title: Biggest Lottery Winners: What Happened After They Won
description: The real stories of America's biggest lottery winners reveal the jackpot was just the beginning. What they did next — and what money couldn't fix.
content:
The Night Everything Changed

Mavis Wanczyk didn't wait until morning. The 53-year-old hospital worker from Chicopee, Massachusetts, checked her numbers on the night of August 23, 2017, and within hours she had done something that most people only imagine: she called her employer and quit on the phone. No two weeks' notice. No farewell party. Just a conversation that ended one chapter of her life and began one so strange and enormous that no one around her — including Mavis herself — was fully prepared for it. She had just won $758.7 million in Powerball, the largest single-ticket jackpot in U.S. history at the time. But the number isn't the story. The phone call is.

That moment — ordinary person, ordinary phone, extraordinary news — is the most human thing about the lottery. Before the lawyers arrive, before the press conference, before the financial advisors and the long-lost relatives, there is just a person standing somewhere unremarkable, holding a piece of paper that has rewritten their life. The biggest lottery winners in American history all passed through that exact moment. What came before it, and what came after, is what this story is really about.

Who They Were Before the Numbers Dropped

Lives Built on Ordinary Tuesdays

Mavis Wanczyk had worked at Mercy Medical Center for 32 years. She was a mother, a grandmother, a woman who bought lottery tickets the way millions of Americans do — casually, hopefully, without real expectation. Gloria MacKenzie, who won a $590.5 million Powerball jackpot in May 2013 in Florida, was 84 years old when her numbers came in. She was, by any measure, already at the end of a long life when fortune intervened. Manuel Franco was 24 years old and working an ordinary job in Wisconsin when he won $768.4 million in Powerball in March 2019. Edwin Castro, whose name became attached to the largest lottery prize in world history, was a relatively private individual living in California when Powerball drew the numbers on November 8, 2022.

What connects these people is not ambition or cleverness or any special relationship with luck. They were nurses' aides and retirees and young men working their way into adulthood. Jack Whittaker was already a successful contractor in West Virginia when he won $314.9 million in Powerball on December 25, 2002 — a Christmas Day jackpot that seemed, at first, like the kind of story you tell your grandchildren. The money arrived not as a reward for struggle, but as a random interruption of normal life. That distinction matters more than it might seem.

The Claim, the Cameras, the Chaos

What the First 72 Hours Actually Looked Like

The public reveal is almost always jarring. Mavis Wanczyk stood at a press conference the day after her win and said, plainly, that she planned to "go hide." She had already quit her job. She took the lump sum — roughly $480 million before taxes — and largely disappeared from public life, which turned out to be one of the more functional decisions any major winner has made. Gloria MacKenzie, at 84, claimed her prize quietly through a trust, as many winners in Florida now do to protect their privacy. The spectacle was minimal by design.

Manuel Franco, by contrast, held a press conference in Wisconsin that was notable for how visibly overwhelmed he appeared. He was 24. The cameras, the questions, the sheer enormity of a number that exceeded anything in his frame of reference — it showed on his face. He said publicly that he planned to invest, travel, and help his family. The specifics were vague in the way that specifics always are when someone hasn't yet had time to think. Edwin Castro's $2.04 billion Powerball win in California — the largest in world history — came with a legal dispute over ticket ownership that played out in the courts, adding a layer of complexity to what might otherwise have been a straightforward claim. He ultimately prevailed, but the case was a reminder that even the cleanest windfall can become complicated fast. For California lottery winners, the state's requirement to go public with the win adds particular pressure in those first hours.

The Most Surprising Thing a Winner Said

"I just want to go hide." — Mavis Wanczyk, at her press conference the day after winning $758.7 million in Powerball, August 2017.

Three words. After 32 years of working hospital shifts, after a lifetime of buying lottery tickets like everyone else, after winning the largest single-ticket jackpot in American history at that point — her first instinct wasn't to celebrate. It was to disappear. There is something in that reaction that the dollar amount alone can never convey.

The Longer Arc: What the Money Did and Didn't Fix

When Fortune Becomes a Weight

Jack Whittaker's story is the one most people cite when they talk about lottery winners and what comes after. His $314.9 million Christmas Day win in 2002 made him the subject of enormous public attention in West Virginia. In the years that followed, he faced a series of documented personal tragedies and legal troubles that became widely reported: burglaries, lawsuits, the deaths of people close to him. He gave away millions to churches and charities. He also reportedly said, in a documented public statement, that he wished he had torn up the ticket. His story is not a simple morality tale — it is something messier and sadder, the account of a man who was already successful and found that more money did not equal more peace.

Gloria MacKenzie, who was already 84 when she claimed her Florida jackpot, used a trust and kept an almost total public silence afterward. At that age, with that approach, she avoided most of the chaos that younger, more visible winners experienced. Mavis Wanczyk similarly retreated, and by most public accounts has maintained a private life since her win. Manuel Franco made several public statements about wanting to help his family and invest wisely, but has largely stayed out of the spotlight. What these winners did with specific assets beyond those public statements is not part of the documented record, and speculation serves no one.

What These Stories Quietly Reveal

Patterns Without a Lecture

Read enough of these accounts and certain things emerge without anyone having to say them directly. The winners who fared best in public life were the ones who moved quickly toward privacy — through legal trusts, through deliberate silence, through the conscious decision not to perform their windfall for an audience. The winners whose stories became complicated often had the complexity imposed on them by circumstance, by other people, by the simple fact that an enormous public number attached to a private name creates pressure that most human beings were never built to handle.

The 2016 $1.586 billion Powerball jackpot — split across three tickets in California, Florida, and Tennessee — produced winners who mostly chose anonymity where state law allowed it. The state lottery laws that govern disclosure vary dramatically, and the decision of where you live when you win turns out to matter almost as much as the numbers themselves. What none of these stories suggests, in the documented record, is that the money solved everything. What they do suggest is that the people who treated the win as a logistical problem to be managed — carefully, quietly, with good counsel — tended to have quieter stories afterward. Whether that counts as a better outcome depends entirely on what you think a good outcome looks like.

Lottery outcomes are entirely random, and winner stories are presented here for informational and entertainment purposes only. Past jackpot results have no bearing on future draws.
